Jay Rosenthal: We have a panel with a bunch of retailers in New York about "co-opetition" — that's the word I'm using, they're in this together whether they like it or not, they may be in competition, but good rules, regulations, and a thoughtful approach to their business helps them all. We've got Vlad Batista and Joanne Wilson from Gotham, and I think one more I can't remember right now, but that's an important conversation. We're having a real conversation about price compression in New York, which is the number one topic there, with Lit Alerts and a couple of different operators, about how they're dealing with it and how a market actually thinks about it, so it's going to be a thoughtful conversation. We heard back from attendees at round one — they said fewer panels, more networking — so we've shrunk it down, it's about an hour, an hour and fifteen of panel conversation and speakers, then an hour and a half to two hours of networking. We're not changing locations this time either — last time we had one place for the panels and a different place for networking, this time we're keeping it all in one location, the Green Room at WNYC in Soho, New York City. It's going to be a great event, I encourage folks to go — you can find it on our website, but you have to go through the Gotham website, Highrise, to register. Tickets are on sale, but we have to unlock it for you, because we want to make sure the room is representative of the industry in New York and elsewhere, so we ask for an application. It's a great event, and then, as I mentioned, we're hitting the road after that — St. Louis, Las Vegas, Buffalo, all before the end of the year. You want to come on the road with us, Bryan?

Bryan Fields: Maybe, depends on the week. But I can tell which regulators are reading Cultivated based on the cities you're going to — I've got my detective hat on, I figured that one out.

Jay Rosenthal: If I were them, I'd read it too. Of course, dude, of course — if you're not reading it, you're probably not doing your job right, because that's part of your job, to understand what's going on and how it all works.

Bryan Fields: One more thing I wanted to point out — the fact that everyone came back and said they wanted more networking, I think, is an incredible sign, because panels are good, but they have a finite amount of value — doesn't matter how amazing you make it — but the networking means people were having really good conversations and didn't want to stop. That's the best sign, because sometimes you go to these events and walk around six times and have maybe one conversation, and the feeling isn't there. The fact that people wanted more of that is a really, really good sign.

Jay Rosenthal: Yeah, I like that too — it's helpful for my business to meet everybody face to face, but it's also indicative, I think, of where the industry is, and how we try to plan our events — people are looking for more intimate settings where everybody's "actionable," which is a weird way to put it, but they're actually meeting people they can do business with, and it's not as direct as a buyer here, a brand there, a retailer here — it's people in the industry, all of a mind that they want to do good work, knowing the rough waters ahead, and when you put those people in a room together, alchemy happens.

Bryan Fields: I love it. Only strong survive. Jay, for our listeners who want to get in touch, want to read Cultivated, and more importantly want to hang out with us at the upcoming event, where can they find you?

Jay Rosenthal: Cultivated.news, easy peasy — hit subscribe, put your email in, you'll get our newsletter every single day, it'll be worth your read. I think the longest one we've ever put out is maybe ten minutes, usually it's between five and seven. I think it's really thoughtful, Jeremy does an unbelievable job as editor-in-chief putting it all together. You can also find us on YouTube, all the links are there — this week we had one of the co-founders of Grown Rogue, we had the lieutenant governor candidate from Texas, and we have a show on Fridays called This Week in Cannabis Live, Bryan, you're going to be on it this Friday I think. We try to have fun, we're still talking about cannabis, so it's "around the horn," that's how I'd describe it.

Bryan Fields: And what about any upcoming big conversations with any MSOs?

Jay Rosenthal: Yeah, I think we're going to have Boris Jordan on — I can't say the date because I don't actually know it, but it's coming up. Also some thoughtful analysis about that deal in particular, because I live in Canada, and it has a different view here than it does on the other side of the border. Also this week the price went up — Curaleaf raised their bid to five dollars a share. If you're not following Cam Battley, who was a C-suite executive at Aurora, he's been tweeting about the deal, and I think really insightfully, as a former Aurora insider and someone who's been in business a long time with publicly traded companies — this isn't his first time watching a hostile takeover and what it all means. I think he's providing some of the best analysis on it, pretty cool story.

Bryan Fields: It's straight out of a TV show.

Jay Rosenthal: It is, and he's sort of curating it like it is a TV show, but he's got an insider's lens, and he's still a shareholder. What strikes me is that Aurora hasn't been, over the past years, super in touch with their investor base, which surprises me, because I know a lot of people spend a lot of time thinking about that — we talk to High Tide all the time, and they're really on top of it, which I think a lot of publicly traded companies should be, lest they find Curaleaf knocking on their door.

Bryan Fields: I love it. Thanks for taking the time, this was a lot of fun.

Jay Rosenthal: This was so much fun, Bryan. We'll see you out and about.
summary: Jay Rosenthal, co-founder of the cannabis industry newsletter Cultivated, joins Bryan Fields to unpack why federal cannabis reform may actually benefit the biggest MSOs more than it threatens them, since their regulatory "moat" widens the longer limbo persists. The conversation ranges across NYSE/NASDAQ listing hurdles, the Curaleaf-Aurora hostile takeover and what it reveals about the future of EU GMP and international markets, how operators like Heirloom and Jointly are winning in New York, and the business model behind building a trusted daily cannabis media brand. It's a wide-ranging look at how federal gridlock, state-level micro-decisions, and media trust are all shaping who actually benefits in today's cannabis industry.
takeaways: Federal 'limbo' isn't necessarily bad for the largest MSOs — it widens their competitive moat, so there's no true united front pushing for reform in DC.
MSOs don't want the same federal reforms because their interests diverge by which states they operate in (e.g., hemp-derived THC vs. traditional cannabis operators).
Credit card processing access is one of the few reforms almost everyone in the industry agrees would help, likely boosting average basket sizes.
Micro-level regulatory decisions (like how many dispensary licenses a small city approves) can have outsized macro effects on a state's overall cannabis market.

The Curaleaf hostile bid for Aurora highlights a strategic pivot toward EU GMP-compliant, internationally focused cannabis businesses (Germany, Israel, Australia) as the more durable model going forward.
Operators with transferable skills from adjacent industries (like Heirloom's hemp/distribution background) tend to outperform cannabis-only operators who had to build everything from scratch.
Potential future FDA/EU GMP-style compliance requirements could favor large, well-capitalized operators and squeeze out smaller companies unable to retrofit facilities.
Cultivated's media business model relies on a three-legged stool of advertising/partnerships, events, and a new membership/subscription tier built on long-form journalism and trust.

faq.question: Why might large cannabis MSOs not be in a rush for federal legalization?
faq.answer: Federal limbo has become part of their business model — the complexity and cost of operating under current rules widens the competitive moat for the biggest, best-capitalized operators, making it harder for smaller players to catch up.

faq.question: Why don't cannabis MSOs present a united front on federal policy like other industries (e.g., beer or pharma)?
faq.answer: Because MSOs operate in different combinations of states with different rules, what benefits one operator (such as hemp-derived THC policy) can directly hurt another, making their interests misaligned despite being the same type of company.

faq.question: What cannabis reform does almost everyone in the industry agree on?
faq.answer: Access to standard credit card processing in dispensaries is one of the few reforms with broad agreement, since it would likely increase average basket sizes at retail.

faq.question: Why is Curaleaf pursuing a hostile takeover of Aurora Cannabis?
faq.answer: Aurora has EU GMP-certified facilities and established medical cannabis distribution in Germany and other international markets, which are seen as more profitable, steadier, and strategically valuable than the fragmented U.S. market, making Aurora's assets a 'crown jewel' acquisition target.

faq.question: What is EU GMP and why does it matter for cannabis companies?
faq.answer: EU GMP (European Union Good Manufacturing Practice) is a strict pharmaceutical-grade compliance standard required to sell cannabis into EU medical markets; facilities built to this standard are expensive and difficult to retrofit, making existing EU GMP-certified operators highly valuable.

faq.question: Why do small, seemingly local regulatory decisions matter to an entire state's cannabis market?
faq.answer: Because cannabis markets are still relatively small overall, decisions like how many dispensary licenses a local planning commission approves in a single city can meaningfully shift statewide sales, job numbers, and how investable the market appears to outsiders.

faq.question: What advantage do operators like Heirloom have over cannabis-only startups?
faq.answer: Heirloom entered cannabis after building infrastructure, distribution relationships, and operational know-how in the hemp space first, meaning they didn't have to build every skill from scratch — giving them a faster, more efficient path to scaling in New York.

faq.question: Why does Jay Rosenthal believe a legal retail cannabis market's success shouldn't be measured by the number of dispensaries?
faq.answer: Using dispensary count or viability as a success metric can be misleading — in Ontario, a flood of new stores drove down black market sales (a policy win) even though many of those same stores later went out of business financially.

faq.question: What is Cultivated's membership model and what does it include?
faq.answer: Cultivated's membership offers roughly four exclusive long-form stories per month, a weekly 'People Moves' industry hiring roundup, discounted and early access to in-person events, and direct briefings with the co-founders, building on their existing free daily newsletter.
